bibl.title: Unsupervised Learning of Persistent and Sequential Activity

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether persistent activity and sequential activity need different learning rules, or are one rule at two settings of the input statistics
span.quote: One unresolved issue is whether the learning rules used by brain networks to learn PA are fundamentally different than the ones used to learn SA, or whether the same learning rule can produce both, depending on the statistics of the inputs to the network. Learning rules employed in theoretical studies to learn PA typically do not contain any temporal asymmetry, while rules used to learn SA need to contain such a temporal asymmetry.

span.label: what conditions a plasticity rule and an input statistic must meet to learn either type of dynamics stably
span.quote: It has been hypothesized that both types of dynamics can be “learned” by the relevant networks from the statistics of their inputs, thanks to mechanisms of synaptic plasticity. However, the necessary conditions for a synaptic plasticity rule and input statistics to learn these two types of dynamics in a stable fashion are still unclear. In particular, it is unclear whether a single learning rule is able to learn both types of activity patterns, depending on the statistics of the inputs driving the network.

span.label: one temporally asymmetric Hebbian rule learns both, with slow stimuli giving persistent activity and fast stimuli sequences - provided a stabilisation mechanism masks the recurrent connections during learning
span.quote: Depending on the stimulus parameters, the network is flexible enough to learn selectively both types of activity by repeated exposure to a sequence of stimuli, without need for supervision. This suggests that cortical circuits endowed with a single learning rule can learn qualitatively different neural dynamics (i.e., persistent vs. sequential activity) depending on the stimuli statistics.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Our network model shows how a network with plastic synapses can stably and flexibly learn PA and SA in an unsupervised manner.

span.label: persistent and sequential delay activity
span.quote: Two strikingly distinct types of activity have been observed in various brain structures during delay periods of delayed response tasks: Persistent activity (PA), in which a sub-population of neurons maintains an elevated firing rate throughout an entire delay period; and Sequential activity (SA), in which sub-populations of neurons are activated sequentially in time.

span.label: simulation
span.quote: We use a rate model to describe the activity of populations of neurons (Wilson and Cowan, 1972 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Homeostatic scaling masks the Hebbian-learned excitatory weights while the stimulus is on and unmasks them afterwards, so the strong connectivity never feeds back into the activity that creates it.
span.quote: We show that a generalized version of the standard multiplicative homeostatic plasticity (Renart et al., 2003 ; Toyoizumi et al., 2014 ) stabilizes learning by effectively masking excitatory connections during stimulation and unmasking those connections during retrieval.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Without a stabilizer, rising synaptic weights raise firing rates which in turn raise the weights, a positive feedback loop that runs away to saturation.
span.quote: This is a consequence of the classic instability observed with Hebbian plasticity rules, where a positive feedback loop between the increase in synaptic connectivity and increase in firing rates leads to an explosive increase in both

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Under synaptic normalization the fixed weight budget forces the very connections that sustain co-active assemblies to be depressed as new co-activations appear, so assemblies keep being rebuilt instead of settling.
span.quote: This leads to complex dynamics in the synaptic weights, in which the connections sustaining co-active neuronal assemblies (i.e., group of excitatory populations with clustered connectivity) learned via Hebbian plasticity are depressed due to the interplay between synaptic normalization and sequential stimulation.

span.label: the stabiliser works by masking the excitatory connections while the stimulus is on and unmasking them at retrieval, so the network cannot drive itself during learning
span.quote: Consistent with previous studies, we find that for stable learning of PA and SA, an additional stabilization mechanism is necessary. We show that a generalized version of the standard multiplicative homeostatic plasticity (Renart et al., 2003 ; Toyoizumi et al., 2014 ) stabilizes learning by effectively masking excitatory connections during stimulation and unmasking those connections during retrieval.

span.label: without it the previously stimulated population is still active when the next one arrives, which strengthens the connection between them until every population is persistently active and every weight is maximal
span.quote: In our model, unsupervised temporally asymmetric Hebbian plasticity is unstable, and after a number of stimulations, all synaptic weights increase to the maximum value. The destabilization occurs during sequential stimulation when the population previously stimulated in the sequence presents persistent activity at the moment the next population is being stimulated. This leads to the increase of the feedforward synaptic weight between these two populations, producing that both present PA while the next population in the sequence is being stimulated. This process continues in each repetition of the sequential stimulation until all populations in the network present PA leading to an increase in the synaptic weights to maximum values.

span.label: and the resulting positive feedback loop is what runs the weights away - more activity, more average synaptic strength, more activity
span.quote: Consistent with many previous studies (Dayan and Abbott, 2001 ), we have shown that a network with unsupervised Hebbian plasticity under sequential stimulation leads to a runaway of the synaptic weights. This instability is due to a positive feed-back loop generated by the progressive increase of network activity leading to a progressive increase in average synaptic strength when PA or SA are being learned.

span.label: with the outcome set by two stimulus parameters alone - long durations and large delays give persistent activity, long durations and short delays give sequences
span.quote: We found that stimulations with long durations and large delays generically leads to the formation of PA, whereas stimulations with long enough durations and short delays leads to the formation of SA. Thus, persistent stimulation leads to persistent activity while sequential stimulation leads to sequential activity.

span.label: The background state of the model sits at zero activity, an artefact of the simplified transfer function.
span.quote: This is an unrealistic feature stemming from the simplified piecewise linear transfer function used in our network (see Equation 5).

span.label: The homeostatic rule operates an order of magnitude faster than experimentally reported homeostasis.
span.quote: Additionally, the timescale of this rule is of the order of minutes (see Figure 8A ), which is an order of magnitude faster of what has been reported experimentally (Turrigiano et al., 1998 ; Turrigiano, 2008 , 2017 ) (see section 3.3 for a discussion).

span.label: Without supervision the network learns only the order of stimuli, not their precise timing.
span.quote: The cost of not having supervision is that the network can only learn the temporal order of the presented stimuli, but not their precise timing.

span.label: A region of the stimulus-parameter space was deliberately not studied.
span.quote: We chose not to study the region corresponding to 2 T + Δ < D here, which is a region where “feedforward” connections involving non-nearest neighbor populations can also increase during learning.

span.label: the background state of the model is zero activity, which the authors call an unrealistic feature stemming from their simplified transfer function
span.quote: Lastly, another difference with the models above, and with classical models for persistent delay activity (Amit and Brunel, 1997 ), is that in our model the “background state” is at zero activity. This is an unrealistic feature stemming from the simplified piecewise linear transfer function used in our network (see Equation 5).

span.label: an unsupervised rule can learn the order of the stimuli but not their timing, and the model that recovers timing needs its parameters precisely related
span.quote: The cost of not having supervision is that the network can only learn the temporal order of the presented stimuli, but not their precise timing. Veliz-Cuba et al. ( 2015 ) have recently provided a model which bear strong similarities with our model (rate model with unsupervised temporally asymmetric Hebbian plasticity rule), but includes in addition a short-term facilitation mechanism that allows the network to learn both order and precise timing of a sequence presented in input. However, their mechanisms require parameters to be precisely related.

span.label: an alternative stabilisation mechanism also works, over different parameter ranges, and those results are not shown
span.quote: We have also tried other stabilization mechanisms such as inhibitory to excitatory plasticity (Vogels et al., 2011 ) instead of homeostatic plasticity. In this case we found that stable learning of PA and SA is possible, but for distinct sets of network and stimulation parameters (data not shown).

span.label: and whether the compensatory timescales this class of model requires exist in real tissue is under active dispute
span.quote: As explained in Zenke and Gerstner ( 2017 ) and Zenke et al. ( 2017 ), in order to prevent the runaway of the synaptic weights produced by Hebbian plasticity, the timescale of any compensatory mechanism should be of the same order or faster than the Hebbian timescale. For generalized homeostatic plasticity, the timescale of the homeostatic variable H i is dependent on the firing rate of neuron i and the target firing rate [i.e., ϕ( u i )/ϕ( u 0 )]. When the network firing rate is close to the target firing rate the homeostatic learning rule is slow, and the homeostatic mechanism seldom play a role in the dynamics. On the other hand, for high firing rates the homeostatic plasticity timescale becomes faster, preventing the runaway of the synaptic weights. There is currently an ongoing debate about whether the timescales of compensatory processes used in theoretical studies, as the ones used here, are consistent with experimental evidence

span.label: a full bifurcation diagram computed for fixed connectivity, then used as the map on which learning is a trajectory
span.quote: Using the bifurcation diagram derived for fixed connectivity, we study analytically the temporal evolution and the steady state of the learned recurrent architecture as a function of parameters characterizing the external inputs. Slow changing stimuli lead to PA, while fast changing stimuli lead to SA. Our network model shows how a network with plastic synapses can stably and flexibly learn PA and SA in an unsupervised manner.

span.label: homeostatic scaling, generalized so that its speed depends on how far the rate is from target
span.quote: As explained in Zenke and Gerstner ( 2017 ) and Zenke et al. ( 2017 ), in order to prevent the runaway of the synaptic weights produced by Hebbian plasticity, the timescale of any compensatory mechanism should be of the same order or faster than the Hebbian timescale. For generalized homeostatic plasticity, the timescale of the homeostatic variable H i is dependent on the firing rate of neuron i and the target firing rate [i.e., ϕ( u i )/ϕ( u 0 )]. When the network firing rate is close to the target firing rate the homeostatic learning rule is slow, and the homeostatic mechanism seldom play a role in the dynamics. On the other hand, for high firing rates the homeostatic plasticity timescale becomes faster, preventing the runaway of the synaptic weights. There is currently an ongoing debate about whether the timescales of compensatory processes used in theoretical studies, as the ones used here, are consistent with experimental evidence

span.label: the supervised/unsupervised division, imported as the axis along which sequence-learning models are classified
span.quote: The models investigated can be roughly divided in two categories: models with supervised and unsupervised plasticity rules. In models with supervised plasticity rules, the synapses are updated according the activity of the network and an error signal that carries information about the difference between the current network dynamics and the one that it is expected to learn by the network (Sussillo and Abbott, 2009 ; Laje and Buonomano, 2013 ; Memmesheimer et al., 2014 ; Rajan et al., 2016 ). In models with unsupervised plasticity rules, sequential dynamics is shaped by external stimulation without an error signal (Jun and Jin, 2007 ; Liu and Buonomano, 2009 ; Fiete et al., 2010 ; Waddington et al., 2012 ; Okubo et al., 2015 ; Veliz-Cuba et al., 2015 ). In those models SA is generated spontaneously, and the temporal statistics of the stimulation shapes the specific timing of the sequences.

span.label: the Wilson-Cowan rate description, chosen because it can be solved rather than only simulated
span.quote: We use a rate model to describe the activity of populations of neurons (Wilson and Cowan, 1972 ). The connectivity in this model represents the average of the synaptic connections between populations of neurons, allowing to investigate at a mesoscopic level the learning mechanisms of PA and SA. This model has the advantage of analytical tractability.

span.label: an instantaneous synaptic normalization tried first, holding the summed incoming weight to each population constant
span.quote: First, we found that by adding to unsupervised Hebbian plasticity an instantaneous synaptic normalization mechanism that maintains constant the sum of incoming synaptic weights to each population, PA and SA cannot be stably learned. Second, we found that adding a generalized homeostatic plasticity to unsupervised Hebbian plasticity leads to stable learning of PA and SA.

span.label: an inhibitory-to-excitatory plasticity rule tried as a third stabiliser
span.quote: We have also tried other stabilization mechanisms such as inhibitory to excitatory plasticity (Vogels et al., 2011 ) instead of homeostatic plasticity. In this case we found that stable learning of PA and SA is possible, but for distinct sets of network and stimulation parameters (data not shown).

span.label: the learning trajectory plotted inside a bifurcation diagram derived beforehand for FIXED connectivity
span.quote: Using the bifurcation diagram derived for fixed connectivity, we study analytically the temporal evolution and the steady state of the learned recurrent architecture as a function of parameters characterizing the external inputs. Slow changing stimuli lead to PA, while fast changing stimuli lead to SA. Our network model shows how a network with plastic synapses can stably and flexibly learn PA and SA in an unsupervised manner.

span.label: synaptic plasticity rule → input statistics
span.note: DECLARED OPEN BY THE PAPER: the necessary conditions for a plasticity rule and input statistics to learn these dynamics stably ARE STILL UNCLEAR, and it is unclear whether one rule can learn both. No edge type can assert that a relation is undetermined; every one of the eight says a relation HOLDS.
span.quote: It has been hypothesized that both types of dynamics can be “learned” by the relevant networks from the statistics of their inputs, thanks to mechanisms of synaptic plasticity. However, the necessary conditions for a synaptic plasticity rule and input statistics to learn these two types of dynamics in a stable fashion are still unclear. In particular, it is unclear whether a single learning rule is able to learn both types of activity patterns, depending on the statistics of the inputs driving the network.

span.label: TWO PHENOMENA CALLED FUNDAMENTALLY DIFFERENT, THEN SHOWN TO BE ONE RULE AT TWO SETTINGS: from a theoretical standpoint the mechanism generating one is FUNDAMENTALLY DIFFERENT from the other - one is a path through state space, the other a fixed point attractor
span.quote: From a theoretical stand point, the mechanism to generate SA is fundamentally different from the one that generates PA. While SA usually corresponds to a path in the state space of the network, PA is identified as a fixed point attractor. Thus, SA has an inherent transient nature while PA is at least linearly stable in a dynamical system sense.

span.label: with the open question posed exactly - are the learning rules fundamentally different, or can THE SAME RULE produce both depending on the statistics of the inputs?
span.quote: One unresolved issue is whether the learning rules used by brain networks to learn PA are fundamentally different than the ones used to learn SA, or whether the same learning rule can produce both, depending on the statistics of the inputs to the network. Learning rules employed in theoretical studies to learn PA typically do not contain any temporal asymmetry, while rules used to learn SA need to contain such a temporal asymmetry.

span.label: AND THE ANSWER IS THE SAME RULE: cortical circuits endowed with A SINGLE LEARNING RULE can learn QUALITATIVELY DIFFERENT neural dynamics depending on the stimuli statistics
span.quote: Depending on the stimulus parameters, the network is flexible enough to learn selectively both types of activity by repeated exposure to a sequence of stimuli, without need for supervision. This suggests that cortical circuits endowed with a single learning rule can learn qualitatively different neural dynamics (i.e., persistent vs. sequential activity) depending on the stimuli statistics.

span.label: with the parameter that decides it named: long durations and large delays give persistent activity, long durations and SHORT delays give sequences - PERSISTENT STIMULATION LEADS TO PERSISTENT ACTIVITY WHILE SEQUENTIAL STIMULATION LEADS TO SEQUENTIAL ACTIVITY
span.quote: We found that stimulations with long durations and large delays generically leads to the formation of PA, whereas stimulations with long enough durations and short delays leads to the formation of SA. Thus, persistent stimulation leads to persistent activity while sequential stimulation leads to sequential activity.

span.label: A CONVENIENCE OF THE MODELLING TRADITION TREATED AS A FACT ABOUT BRAINS: earlier models SEPARATED a learning phase in which recurrent dynamics was SHUT DOWN from a retrieval phase in which the connectivity no longer changes - and that separation is called THE DRAWBACK OF THESE MODELS
span.quote: The drawback of these models is that they separated a learning phase in which recurrent dynamics was shut down in order to form the synaptic connectivity matrix, and a retrieval phase in which the connectivity matrix does not change anymore. Our model removes this artificial separation, since both plasticity rule and recurrent dynamics operate continuously, both during learning and recall. However, we found that there needs to be a mechanism to attenuate recurrent dynamics during learning for it to be stable.

span.label: with the honest version stated - by compartmentalizing dynamics and learning in time the runaway is prevented, but IT IS UNCLEAR WHETHER SUCH COMPARTMENTALIZATION EXISTS IN CORTICAL NETWORKS
span.quote: Therefore, by compartmentalizing in time dynamics and learning, the network dynamics does not lead to changes in the synaptic weights during retrieval, and conversely, changes in synaptic weights do not lead to changes in the dynamics during learning. This separation prevents the observed runaway of the synaptic weights due to unsupervised Hebbian plasticity. However, it is unclear whether such compartmentalization exists in cortical networks. In this work, we explored the alternative scenario, in which both plasticity and dynamics happen concurrently during learning and retrieval

span.label: A DISAGREEMENT WITH PRIOR MODELS DIAGNOSED TO ONE PARAMETER: earlier work learned persistent activity WITHOUT any stabiliser, and the key difference is that in those models the persistent rate sits BELOW THE THRESHOLD FOR LTP INDUCTION, where here it is always maximal
span.quote: However, previous studies have shown that PA could be learned without additional stabilization mechanisms. In Del Giudice and Mattia ( 2001 ), Del Giudice et al. ( 2003 ), and Mongillo et al. ( 2005 ) PA is learnt without any stabilizing mechanism except for short-term depression. These studies have a number of differences with ours, however, we believe the key difference for stable learning PA is that in these models there is PA (in the absence of inputs to the network) below the threshold for LTP induction - something is not currently present in our model since PA is always at the maximal rate. Therefore, unlike our model, PA after stimulation does not lead to effective changes in the synaptic connections.

span.label: and the thresholds are SET so that there is no learning when both populations are persistently active - a modelling choice that decides whether a stabiliser is needed at all
span.quote: Importantly, as in the previous models discussed above, the learning thresholds are set in such a way that there is no learning when both populations present PA. Additionally, during learning the presentations of stimuli are far apart, and unlike our model learning feedback and feedforward connections are due to persistent activity in one neuron, and the stimulation in the other, followed by a small increase in the synaptic strengths in each presentation.

span.label: with the two mechanisms recognised as the same move under different names - short-term depression shuts down high firing rates during stimulation, WHICH RESEMBLES THE EFFECT of the homeostatic rule here
span.quote: Interestingly, they introduced short term depression to stabilize learning by rapidly shutting down high firing rates during stimulation or PA, which resembles the effect of the generalized homeostatic plasticity rule in our model.

span.label: AN UNREALISTIC FEATURE DECLARED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: the background state is at zero activity, AN UNREALISTIC FEATURE STEMMING FROM THE SIMPLIFIED PIECEWISE LINEAR TRANSFER FUNCTION
span.quote: Lastly, another difference with the models above, and with classical models for persistent delay activity (Amit and Brunel, 1997 ), is that in our model the “background state” is at zero activity. This is an unrealistic feature stemming from the simplified piecewise linear transfer function used in our network (see Equation 5).

span.label: AND THE PRICE OF NO SUPERVISION IS NAMED: the network can learn the TEMPORAL ORDER of the stimuli BUT NOT THEIR PRECISE TIMING - and the model that recovers timing REQUIRES PARAMETERS TO BE PRECISELY RELATED
span.quote: The cost of not having supervision is that the network can only learn the temporal order of the presented stimuli, but not their precise timing. Veliz-Cuba et al. ( 2015 ) have recently provided a model which bear strong similarities with our model (rate model with unsupervised temporally asymmetric Hebbian plasticity rule), but includes in addition a short-term facilitation mechanism that allows the network to learn both order and precise timing of a sequence presented in input. However, their mechanisms require parameters to be precisely related.

span.label: with the other side of that trade priced too - supervised rules reproduce target sequences PERFECTLY, and ARE NOT BIOPHYSICALLY REALISTIC
span.quote: Models with supervised learning can reproduce perfectly target sequences through minimization of a suitable error function (Sussillo and Abbott, 2009 ; Laje and Buonomano, 2013 ; Memmesheimer et al., 2014 ; Rajan et al., 2016 ), but the corresponding learning rules are not biophysically realistic.

span.label: THE FIRST STABILISER TRIED DID NOT WORK, AND IS REPORTED: instantaneous synaptic normalization holding the summed input weight constant does NOT give stable learning, and the homeostatic rule does
span.quote: First, we found that by adding to unsupervised Hebbian plasticity an instantaneous synaptic normalization mechanism that maintains constant the sum of incoming synaptic weights to each population, PA and SA cannot be stably learned. Second, we found that adding a generalized homeostatic plasticity to unsupervised Hebbian plasticity leads to stable learning of PA and SA.

span.label: and a third mechanism works too, over DISTINCT sets of parameters - DATA NOT SHOWN
span.quote: We have also tried other stabilization mechanisms such as inhibitory to excitatory plasticity (Vogels et al., 2011 ) instead of homeostatic plasticity. In this case we found that stable learning of PA and SA is possible, but for distinct sets of network and stimulation parameters (data not shown).

span.label: AND THE MODEL'S OWN REQUIREMENT IS UNDER DISPUTE IN THE LITERATURE: the compensatory timescale must be as fast as the Hebbian one, and THERE IS CURRENTLY AN ONGOING DEBATE about whether such timescales are consistent with experimental evidence
span.quote: As explained in Zenke and Gerstner ( 2017 ) and Zenke et al. ( 2017 ), in order to prevent the runaway of the synaptic weights produced by Hebbian plasticity, the timescale of any compensatory mechanism should be of the same order or faster than the Hebbian timescale. For generalized homeostatic plasticity, the timescale of the homeostatic variable H i is dependent on the firing rate of neuron i and the target firing rate [i.e., ϕ( u i )/ϕ( u 0 )]. When the network firing rate is close to the target firing rate the homeostatic learning rule is slow, and the homeostatic mechanism seldom play a role in the dynamics. On the other hand, for high firing rates the homeostatic plasticity timescale becomes faster, preventing the runaway of the synaptic weights. There is currently an ongoing debate about whether the timescales of compensatory processes used in theoretical studies, as the ones used here, are consistent with experimental evidence

span.label: with the instability itself traced to a positive feedback loop - more activity gives more average synaptic strength gives more activity, RUNAWAY of the weights
span.quote: Consistent with many previous studies (Dayan and Abbott, 2001 ), we have shown that a network with unsupervised Hebbian plasticity under sequential stimulation leads to a runaway of the synaptic weights. This instability is due to a positive feed-back loop generated by the progressive increase of network activity leading to a progressive increase in average synaptic strength when PA or SA are being learned.

span.label: and the model chosen for a stated reason - a rate model at the mesoscopic level, with THE ADVANTAGE OF ANALYTICAL TRACTABILITY
span.quote: We use a rate model to describe the activity of populations of neurons (Wilson and Cowan, 1972 ). The connectivity in this model represents the average of the synaptic connections between populations of neurons, allowing to investigate at a mesoscopic level the learning mechanisms of PA and SA. This model has the advantage of analytical tractability.

span.label: extends → the standard multiplicative homeostatic plasticity rule of Renart et al. (2003) and Toyoizumi et al. (2014)
span.quote: We term this rule generalized homeostatic plasticity since is a non-linear generalization of the standard multiplicative homeostatic plasticity rule in Renart et al. ( 2003 ) and Toyoizumi et al. ( 2014 ).

span.label: replicates → the runaway-instability result for unsupervised Hebbian plasticity (Dayan and Abbott, 2001)
span.quote: Consistent with many previous studies (Dayan and Abbott, 2001 ), we have shown that a network with unsupervised Hebbian plasticity under sequential stimulation leads to a runaway of the synaptic weights.

span.label: extends → early binary-neuron sequence models that separated a learning phase from a retrieval phase (Kuhn and van Hemmen, 1991; Herz et al., 1988)
span.quote: Our model removes this artificial separation, since both plasticity rule and recurrent dynamics operate continuously, both during learning and recall.

span.label: contradicts → the assumption that persistent and sequential activity require fundamentally different learning rules
span.note: differs in: depending on the statistics of the inputs driving the network
span.quote: Depending on the stimulus parameters, the network is flexible enough to learn selectively both types of activity by repeated exposure to a sequence of stimuli, without need for supervision. This suggests that cortical circuits endowed with a single learning rule can learn qualitatively different neural dynamics (i.e., persistent vs. sequential activity) depending on the stimuli statistics.

span.label: reconciles → earlier models that learned persistent activity with no stabilisation mechanism at all
span.note: differs in: in these models there is PA (in the absence of inputs to the network) below the threshold for LTP induction
span.quote: However, previous studies have shown that PA could be learned without additional stabilization mechanisms. In Del Giudice and Mattia ( 2001 ), Del Giudice et al. ( 2003 ), and Mongillo et al. ( 2005 ) PA is learnt without any stabilizing mechanism except for short-term depression. These studies have a number of differences with ours, however, we believe the key difference for stable learning PA is that in these models there is PA (in the absence of inputs to the network) below the threshold for LTP induction - something is not currently present in our model since PA is always at the maximal rate. Therefore, unlike our model, PA after stimulation does not lead to effective changes in the synaptic connections.

span.label: critiques → the separation of a learning phase from a retrieval phase, which prevents the instability but may not exist in cortex
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS WHETHER LEARNING AND RETRIEVAL ARE SEPARATED BY HAND. 'THE DRAWBACK OF THESE MODELS IS THAT THEY SEPARATED A LEARNING PHASE IN WHICH RECURRENT DYNAMICS WAS SHUT DOWN in order to form the synaptic connectivity matrix, AND A RETRIEVAL PHASE IN WHICH THE CONNECTIVITY MATRIX DOES NOT CHANGE ANYMORE.' The separation is what keeps those models stable, so it is not an incidental simplification - removing it is the paper's contribution and the reason its result is not comparable. Q-507.
span.quote: The drawback of these models is that they separated a learning phase in which recurrent dynamics was shut down in order to form the synaptic connectivity matrix, and a retrieval phase in which the connectivity matrix does not change anymore. Our model removes this artificial separation, since both plasticity rule and recurrent dynamics operate continuously, both during learning and recall. However, we found that there needs to be a mechanism to attenuate recurrent dynamics during learning for it to be stable.

span.label: distinguishes-from → supervised sequence learning, which reproduces targets perfectly and is not biophysically realistic
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS WHAT THE MODEL BUYS ITS ACCURACY WITH. 'MODELS WITH SUPERVISED LEARNING CAN REPRODUCE PERFECTLY TARGET SEQUENCES through minimization of a suitable error function, BUT THE CORRESPONDING LEARNING RULES ARE NOT BIOPHYSICALLY REALISTIC.' Perfect reproduction is granted and priced: the two classes are not better and worse at the same thing, they are optimising different things. Its [25] in this corpus carries the other side - the unsupervised cost is that only ORDER is learned, not precise timing. Q-496.
span.quote: Models with supervised learning can reproduce perfectly target sequences through minimization of a suitable error function (Sussillo and Abbott, 2009 ; Laje and Buonomano, 2013 ; Memmesheimer et al., 2014 ; Rajan et al., 2016 ), but the corresponding learning rules are not biophysically realistic.

span.label: supports → short-term depression and homeostatic scaling as the same stabilising move under different names
span.quote: Interestingly, they introduced short term depression to stabilize learning by rapidly shutting down high firing rates during stimulation or PA, which resembles the effect of the generalized homeostatic plasticity rule in our model.

span.label: predicts → that slow input statistics produce persistent activity and fast ones produce sequences in cortical circuits
span.quote: We found that stimulations with long durations and large delays generically leads to the formation of PA, whereas stimulations with long enough durations and short delays leads to the formation of SA. Thus, persistent stimulation leads to persistent activity while sequential stimulation leads to sequential activity.

span.label: RETRACTED (THE SPAN STATES AN OPEN QUESTION AND POINTS THE OTHER WAY) · learning rule —causes→ statistics
span.note: RETRACTED: THE SPAN STATES AN OPEN QUESTION AND POINTS THE OTHER WAY. The edge asserts `learning rule --causes--> statistics`. The span says dynamics are learned 'FROM THE STATISTICS of their inputs' - statistics are the input to learning, not its product - and then declares the matter unsettled twice: 'the necessary conditions ... ARE STILL UNCLEAR' and 'it is UNCLEAR WHETHER a single learning rule is able to learn both types'. The only EFFECT cue is `driv`, inside 'the inputs DRIVING the network', which is about the inputs and not about either endpoint's relation to the other. WHAT THE SPAN DOES SAY (Q-309): that the relation is UNKNOWN, housed below - the schema has no way to record an explicitly open question, which is the polarity gap in another form. — strength of the relation: 1 — the question posed exactly - IS A SINGLE LEARNING RULE ABLE TO LEARN BOTH types of activity, depending on the statistics of the inputs driving the network?

However, the necessary conditions for a synaptic plasticity rule and input statistics to learn these two types of dynamics in a stable fashion are still unclear. In particular, it is unclear whether a single learning rule is able to learn both types of activity patterns, depending on the statistics of the inputs driving the network.

HOWEVER, the necessary conditions for a synaptic plasticity rule and input statistics to learn these two types...' A hypothesis of the field, immediately qualified by this paper as having unestablished conditions - which is what the paper exists to work out. A reader joining on `X --causes--> Y` takes it as a causal relation this paper reports. Q-392. — strength of the relation: 1

We show that a generalized version of the standard multiplicative homeostatic plasticity (Renart et al., 2003 ; Toyoizumi et al., 2014 ) stabilizes learning by effectively masking excitatory connections during stimulation and unmasking those connections during retrieval.

In models with supervised plasticity rules, the synapses are updated according the activity of the network and an error signal that carries information about the difference between the current network dynamics and the one that it is expected to learn by the network (Sussillo and Abbott, 2009 ; Laje and Buonomano, 2013 ; Memmesheimer et al., 2014 ; Rajan et al., 2016 ). In models with unsupervised plasticity rules, sequential dynamics is shaped by external stimulation without an error signal (Jun and Jin, 2007 ; Liu and Buonomano, 2009 ; Fiete et al., 2010 ; Waddington et al., 2012 ; Okubo et al., 2015 ; Veliz-Cuba et al., 2015 ). In those models SA is generated spontaneously, and the temporal statistics of the stimulation shapes the specific timing of the sequences.

span.label: persistent activity (PA)
span.quote: Two strikingly distinct types of activity have been observed in various brain structures during delay periods of delayed response tasks: Persistent activity (PA), in which a sub-population of neurons maintains an elevated firing rate throughout an entire delay period; and Sequential activity (SA), in which sub-populations of neurons are activated sequentially in time.

span.label: sequential activity (SA)
span.quote: Two strikingly distinct types of activity have been observed in various brain structures during delay periods of delayed response tasks: Persistent activity (PA), in which a sub-population of neurons maintains an elevated firing rate throughout an entire delay period; and Sequential activity (SA), in which sub-populations of neurons are activated sequentially in time.

span.label: decaying sequence of activity (dSA)
span.quote: When both recurrent and feedforward connections are weak enough (i.e., w + s < 1/ν) the activity decays to zero firing rate fixed point, after a transient in which different populations are transiently activated—a pattern which we term decaying sequence of activity or dSA.

span.label: generalized homeostatic plasticity rule
span.quote: Therefore, we term this rule generalized homeostatic plasticity rule, since this rule is a generalization of the standard multiplicative homeostatic plasticity rule in Renart et al.

span.label: persistent activity
span.quote: From a theoretical stand point, the mechanism to generate SA is fundamentally different from the one that generates PA. While SA usually corresponds to a path in the state space of the network, PA is identified as a fixed point attractor. Thus, SA has an inherent transient nature while PA is at least linearly stable in a dynamical system sense.

span.label: stabilization
span.quote: Consistent with previous studies, we find that for stable learning of PA and SA, an additional stabilization mechanism is necessary. We show that a generalized version of the standard multiplicative homeostatic plasticity (Renart et al., 2003 ; Toyoizumi et al., 2014 ) stabilizes learning by effectively masking excitatory connections during stimulation and unmasking those connections during retrieval.

span.label: runaway
span.quote: Consistent with many previous studies (Dayan and Abbott, 2001 ), we have shown that a network with unsupervised Hebbian plasticity under sequential stimulation leads to a runaway of the synaptic weights. This instability is due to a positive feed-back loop generated by the progressive increase of network activity leading to a progressive increase in average synaptic strength when PA or SA are being learned.

span.label: unsupervised
span.quote: The models investigated can be roughly divided in two categories: models with supervised and unsupervised plasticity rules. In models with supervised plasticity rules, the synapses are updated according the activity of the network and an error signal that carries information about the difference between the current network dynamics and the one that it is expected to learn by the network (Sussillo and Abbott, 2009 ; Laje and Buonomano, 2013 ; Memmesheimer et al., 2014 ; Rajan et al., 2016 ). In models with unsupervised plasticity rules, sequential dynamics is shaped by external stimulation without an error signal (Jun and Jin, 2007 ; Liu and Buonomano, 2009 ; Fiete et al., 2010 ; Waddington et al., 2012 ; Okubo et al., 2015 ; Veliz-Cuba et al., 2015 ). In those models SA is generated spontaneously, and the temporal statistics of the stimulation shapes the specific timing of the sequences.

span.quote: The specific point of the steady state in the bifurcation diagram depends solely on the stimulation parameters—stimulation period T and time delay Δ—and the connectivity initial conditions.

span.quote: In this model, we identify the regions in the connectivity parameter space where SA, PA, or decaying sequences of activity (dSA) are generated.

span.label: type of dynamics the network retrieves after learning (PA, SA, SA/PA or dSA)

span.quote: Throughout this paper, for testing whether PA, SA, SA/PA, or dSA is learned, after sequential stimulation we stimulate the first population and then check whether the network recalls the corresponding type of activity

span.label: inhibitory population time constant
span.quote: For the sake of simplicity we set the inhibitory population dynamics as instantaneous compared with the excitatory timescale.

span.label: stimulation amplitude
span.quote: Each stimulus in the sequence has the same magnitude, that is larger than the learning threshold

span.label: stimulation
span.quote: We found that stimulations with long durations and large delays generically leads to the formation of PA, whereas stimulations with long enough durations and short delays leads to the formation of SA. Thus, persistent stimulation leads to persistent activity while sequential stimulation leads to sequential activity.

span.label: threshold
span.quote: However, previous studies have shown that PA could be learned without additional stabilization mechanisms. In Del Giudice and Mattia ( 2001 ), Del Giudice et al. ( 2003 ), and Mongillo et al. ( 2005 ) PA is learnt without any stabilizing mechanism except for short-term depression. These studies have a number of differences with ours, however, we believe the key difference for stable learning PA is that in these models there is PA (in the absence of inputs to the network) below the threshold for LTP induction - something is not currently present in our model since PA is always at the maximal rate. Therefore, unlike our model, PA after stimulation does not lead to effective changes in the synaptic connections.

span.label: timescale
span.quote: As explained in Zenke and Gerstner ( 2017 ) and Zenke et al. ( 2017 ), in order to prevent the runaway of the synaptic weights produced by Hebbian plasticity, the timescale of any compensatory mechanism should be of the same order or faster than the Hebbian timescale. For generalized homeostatic plasticity, the timescale of the homeostatic variable H i is dependent on the firing rate of neuron i and the target firing rate [i.e., ϕ( u i )/ϕ( u 0 )]. When the network firing rate is close to the target firing rate the homeostatic learning rule is slow, and the homeostatic mechanism seldom play a role in the dynamics. On the other hand, for high firing rates the homeostatic plasticity timescale becomes faster, preventing the runaway of the synaptic weights. There is currently an ongoing debate about whether the timescales of compensatory processes used in theoretical studies, as the ones used here, are consistent with experimental evidence

span.label: two parameters — the duration of stimulus presentations and the interval between them - the whole difference between learning one dynamic and the other reduces to these
span.quote: Here, we hypothesize that a single learning rule is able to learn both, depending on the statistics of the inputs. We investigate what are the conditions for the plasticity mechanisms and external stimulation to learn PA or SA using unsupervised plasticity rules. We consider a model composed of multiple populations of excitatory neurons, each activated by a distinct stimulus. We consider a sequential stimulation protocol in which each population of neurons is stimulated one at a time, one after the other. This protocol is characterized by two parameters, the duration of stimulus presentations and the time interval between stimulations. This simple setting allows us to explore between the extremes of isolated stimulations with short or large duration and sequential stimulations close or far apart temporally.

span.label: bifurcation diagram
span.quote: Using the bifurcation diagram derived for fixed connectivity, we study analytically the temporal evolution and the steady state of the learned recurrent architecture as a function of parameters characterizing the external inputs. Slow changing stimuli lead to PA, while fast changing stimuli lead to SA. Our network model shows how a network with plastic synapses can stably and flexibly learn PA and SA in an unsupervised manner.
